conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time today. My name is Dr. Flores, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I specialize in helping new mothers sort through the emotional ups and downs that can show up after a baby arrives.

To get a quick snapshot of how you’ve been feeling, I’d like to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days, and it helps us see whether you might be dealing with something more than the normal “baby blues.” Everything you share stays confidential between you, me, and the small medical team directly involved in your care. There’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever is true for you.

We’ll take it one question at a time. Ready to begin?

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I… it’s been hard, actually. I used to laugh at little things my husband said or at funny shows, but lately, even when I hear something that should be funny, it just feels flat. I might smile a little, but it’s like I can’t really feel it the way I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, maybe once or twice I sort of half-smiled, but most of the time nothing feels funny. My sister sent me a silly video she swore would crack me up, and I just stared at it feeling blank. It’s like I’m too tired or too… heavy inside to laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I… no, not really. Even little things I used to get excited about—like my favorite show dropping a new episode or planning coffee with my best friend—just feel like chores now. The only thing I really look forward to is maybe getting an hour of quiet when the baby finally sleeps, but even that feels more like relief than actual joy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right, or I missed some cue. Last night he wouldn’t settle and I just kept thinking, “Other moms know how to fix this; why can’t I?” I ended up crying in the rocker, telling myself I’m failing him. Even when my husband says the baby’s just being a baby, I still feel like it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much every day. My heart races the moment I hear him make any noise, and I’m constantly checking if he’s breathing in the bassinet. Sometimes I’ll stand over him for ages, just watching his chest rise and fall. And then I worry that hovering like that means I’m already a “helicopter mom,” and I feel worse. Even when everything’s quiet, there’s this knot in my stomach like something bad is about to happen. It’s exhausting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Most days, yeah. It’s like this sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen to the baby. Sometimes it hits when I’m just folding laundry; out of nowhere my heart’s pounding and I’m scanning the room for dangers that aren’t even there. It passes after a few minutes, but it keeps coming back.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. A lot of the time I feel like I’m drowning in bottles, diapers, and laundry, and no matter how much I do there’s always more. When he cries and I can’t settle him right away, I get this tight feeling in my chest and think, “I can’t do this.” I manage to get through the basics, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby. I replay every little thing I did wrong that day, convince myself he’s going to wake up any second, and then I’m wide awake. Even when he’s sleeping a four-hour stretch, I’ll wake up on my own, heart racing, and stare at the ceiling until I finally drift off right before he needs me again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I wake up feeling like there’s a gray cloud hanging over me, and it just stays. Little things—seeing the pile of laundry or hearing another mom rave about how “blissful” new motherhood is—makes my chest ache. I cry in the shower so my husband won’t notice, then feel guilty for wasting water and for not savoring these “precious newborn days.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it’s been happening a few times a week. Sometimes it’s when I’m nursing at 3 a.m. and feel completely alone; other times it’s when someone just asks, “How are you doing?” and I realize I’m not okay. Yesterday I burst into tears because I dropped a clean burp cloth on the floor and couldn’t bend down to pick it up without waking the baby. It feels so stupid afterward, but in the moment it’s like the tears just take over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I’ve never thought about hurting myself. When things feel really low, I remind myself I have to stay here for my baby, but the idea of actually harming myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

It sounds like these first weeks with your baby have felt overwhelmingly heavy. You described losing the spark that used to make you laugh, feeling as though even simple pleasures are now chores, and carrying a constant knot of worry about your son's safety. The sadness seems to settle in first thing each morning, and the panic waves can appear while you're simply folding laundry. I hear how hard you're trying-checking on his breathing, pushing through feeds, keeping the basics going-and still feeling as if you're drowning.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh, feeling blank at humor, and emotional heaviness matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory joy, equating even former pleasures to chores and only experiencing relief, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('a lot,' 'immediately think it's because I'm doing something wrong') with persistent guilt despite reassurance, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences near-constant, unprovoked anxiety with physical symptoms (heart racing) multiple times daily, meeting 'Yes, very often' criteria</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms and persistent worry about the baby, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "a lot of the time," unable to keep up with basic tasks, and experiencing physical anxiety when soothing fails, indicating frequent inability to cope.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing anxious thoughts, waking with heart racing, confirming 'most of the time' severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily sadness, pervasive low mood, and frequent crying—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "a few times a week" in multiple contexts, matching "Yes, quite often" rather than "most of the time".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 26 places you well above the high-risk cut-off (≥14). You endorsed core symptoms that align with <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: marked <sym>anhedonia</sym> (<quote>nothing feels funny… just feel blank</quote>), <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day (<quote>gray cloud hanging over me</quote>), <sym>guilt</sym> and feelings of inadequacy, <sym>recurrent panic</sym> without clear triggers, and <sym>insomnia</sym> linked to rumination. Frequency and intensity meet DSM-5 criteria when combined with functional impairment. Item 10 was negative, indicating no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>OB-GYN</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review these results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>; many centers offer mother-baby day programs or telehealth therapy
3. Share these EPDS findings with a trusted support person so they can help coordinate appointments and assist with night-time baby care while you rest
4. Begin gentle <med>sleep hygiene</med>: short afternoon rest, dim lights after feeds, delegate one night bottle to partner or support person
5. Consider an online PPD support group or moderated forum for peer encouragement while awaiting professional treatment
6. Keep the baby-care expectations small: aim for one manageable task per day and accept help with dishes, meals, and laundry
7. Maintain brief daily check-ins via text or call with your clinician until treatment is started; report any new thoughts of self-harm immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤12 wks post-delivery  
Instrument: Edinburgh-based clinical interview (10-item)  
Date: [today]

Symptoms / Behaviors Endorsed  
- Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter, anticipatory joy absent  
- Daily depressed mood, frequent crying (≥3×/wk)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care  
- Persistent, intrusive anxiety: heart-racing, breathlessness, catastrophic worries re infant safety  
- Panic-type episodes without clear trigger  
- Subjective “drowning,” difficulty coping with routine tasks  
- Sleep-onset & maintenance insomnia linked to rumination  
- Fatigue described as “heavy inside,” “exhausting”  

Pattern  
Consistent low mood and loss of pleasure, coupled with prominent postpartum-specific anxiety/panic; functional impact on sleep, self-care, and caregiving confidence; no self-harm ideation reported.

Screening Significance  
High clinical likelihood of major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety features; meets EPDS high-risk cut-off on items 1–9 (item 10 negative).

Risk Factors Flagged  
- Persistent sadness, anhedonia, guilt  
- Mood-related insomnia  
- Recurrent panic-type episodes  
- Subjective inability to cope / feeling “drowning”  
- No suicidal thoughts endorsed (safety factor negative) → continue routine safety monitoring

Overall  
Screening indicates probable significant postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms warranting prompt formal evaluation and possible referral to maternal–mental-health specialty services.
